# The Annotated Archive

A shoebox of photographs is not an archive. It is a pile of evidence waiting for a witness. The transformation from storage to meaning happens only when someone explains what the objects are, and this explanation is the part families almost never do in time.

Consider what actually sits in a typical family collection. A black-and-white photograph of a man leaning against a car. A baptismal certificate. A recipe card stained at one corner. A watch that no longer runs. Each of these objects is legible in a limited way: the photograph has a date stamped on the back, perhaps, and the certificate has names and a parish. But the questions that matter—why the man looks so proud of that particular car, why the recipe calls for twice as much salt as seems reasonable, who gave the watch and on what occasion—these answers live only in memory, and memory is not distributed evenly.
